Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 58, verse 1:

Surat al-Mujadila

Madaniyya (Medinan), and it has twenty-two verses.

﴿Indeed, Allah has heard﴾ with the dal made clear (idhhar); it is also read with the dal assimilated into the sin (idgham).

﴿the statement of her who disputes with you concerning her husband﴾ i.e., she argues with you over his affair and over what had proceeded from him against her in the matter of zihar (the pre-Islamic divorce formula of likening one's wife to one's mother). It is also read "tuhawiruka" and "tuhawiluka," meaning: she questions you.

﴿and complains to Allah﴾ is conjoined (atf) to "tujadiluka," i.e., she humbles herself before Him, the Exalted. It has also been said that it is a circumstantial clause (hal) referring to its subject, i.e., she argues with you while humbling herself before Allah, the Exalted. She is Khawla bint Tha'laba ibn Malik ibn Khuzama al-Khazrajiyya. Her husband Aws ibn al-Samit, the brother of 'Ubada, made zihar against her, then regretted what he had said and told her: "I do not think you are anything but forbidden to me." This distressed her, so she sought a ruling from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. He said: "You have become forbidden to him." She said: "O Messenger of Allah, he did not mention divorce." He said: "You have become forbidden to him." — and in another narration: "I do not see you but that you have become forbidden to him in all instances." She said: "I complain to Allah of my poverty and my grief," and she kept returning to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. Whenever he, peace and blessings be upon him, said, "You have become forbidden to him," she cried out and complained to Allah, the Exalted, until it was revealed.

The word "qad" (indeed) indicates that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and the woman who disputed were both expecting that Allah, the Exalted, would reveal the ruling of the incident and relieve her distress, as is hinted at by what is narrated: that when she sought a ruling, he, peace and blessings be upon him, said to her, "I have nothing concerning your matter," and that she would raise her head to the sky and say, "I complain to You; so send down (a ruling) upon the tongue of Your Prophet."

The meaning of His, the Exalted's, hearing her statement is the answering of her supplication, not merely His knowledge of that, as is intended by His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And Allah hears your exchange﴾, i.e., He knows your mutual argument. The use of the present tense indicates the continuity of hearing in accordance with the continuity and renewal of the exchange. Placing her within the address (khitab) by way of precedence (taghlib) is an honour for her in two respects. The sentence is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) serving as a reason (ta'lil) for what precedes it, for her persistence in the question, her exaggeration in humbling herself before Allah, the Exalted, and her insistence upon him, peace and blessings be upon him, with a response indicating hesitation and awaiting revelation, together with Allah's knowledge of her condition, are among the motives for answering. It has been said: (p-216)

It is a circumstantial clause (hal), but this is far-fetched. His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿Indeed, Allah is All-Hearing, All-Seeing﴾ is a reason for what precedes it by way of affirmation (tahqiq), i.e., He is exceedingly knowing of what is heard and what is seen. Among the requirements of this is that He hears their exchange and sees what accompanies it of states, among which is her raising her head to the sky and the rest of the signs of humble supplication. The display of the noble Name in both places serves to cultivate awe, to ground the ruling in the attribute of divinity (uluhiyya), and to emphasize the independence of the two sentences.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 58, verse 2:

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Those of you who divorce their wives by zihar (a pre-Islamic form of divorce in which a husband declares his wife to be like his mother's back)﴾, this begins an explanation of the matter of zihar in itself and of the ruling that follows from it in the Sharia, by way of a fresh statement. Zihar is that a man says to his wife, "You are to me like the back of my mother," and it is derived from "the back" (zahr). Its details have already been explained in Surah al-Ahzab. The jurists have also attached to it the likening of a wife to any other forbidden part of a woman's body. The phrase "of you" (minkum) carries an added rebuke to the Arabs and a condemnation of their custom in this matter, for it was one of the oaths of the people of their pre-Islamic ignorance specifically, and not of the other nations. It has been read as "yazzahharuna" and as "yazharuna." His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿their wives are not their mothers﴾, is the predicate of the relative pronoun, meaning: their wives are not, in actual reality, their mothers, so the claim is pure falsehood. It has also been read as "ummahatuhum" with the nominative, according to the dialect of Tamim, and as "bi-ummahatihim."

﴿Their mothers are not﴾, that is: they are not.

﴿Except those who bore them﴾, so they are not likened to them in prohibition, except for those whom the Sharia has attached to them, namely the wet-nurses and the wives of the Prophet (ﷺ), who by this enter into the ruling of mothers. As for wives, they are the furthest thing from motherhood.

﴿And indeed they utter﴾ by their saying that.

﴿an abominable word and a falsehood﴾. The emphasis here lies not in the utterance proceeding from them, for that is a settled matter, but in its being abominable, that is, in the eyes of the Sharia, of reason and of human nature as well, as its indefinite form indicates. A parallel is His saying: ﴿Indeed you utter a grave word﴾.

﴿And falsehood﴾, that is, distorted from the truth.

﴿Indeed Allah is Pardoning and Forgiving﴾, that is, He is exceedingly forgiving and pardoning, so He forgives what has passed from them absolutely, or by their repentance from it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 58, verse 3:

And His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And those who declare their wives unlawful (yuzahiruna, from zihar) and then wish to go back on what they said﴾: this is a detailing of the ruling on zihar (the pre-Islamic divorce formula of declaring one's wife unlawful like one's mother's back), after the explanation that it is a reprehensible matter, through the general legislative manner that organizes the case in an initial arrangement. That is: those who say that reprehensible statement and then go back on what they said, i.e., return to what they said by making amends and rectification, not by affirming and repeating it, as in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿that you should never return to its like﴾. The lam (ل) and "ila" (إلى) often interchange, as in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿He guided us to this (hadha)﴾, and His saying: ﴿because your Lord has inspired her (awha laha)﴾, and His saying: ﴿and it was revealed to Noah (uhiya ila Nuh)﴾.

﴿then the freeing of a neck (fa-tahriru raqabah)﴾: that is, then making amends for it, or upon him, or the obligation is the freeing of a neck, any neck whatsoever. According to al-Shafi'i, may God have mercy on him, belief (iman) is a condition. The fa' (ف) indicates causation, and among its benefits is the indication that the obligation of freeing recurs with the recurrence of zihar. It has been said that "what they said" is an expression for what they forbade upon themselves by the wording of zihar, treating the saying as if it were the thing said about, as mentioned in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and We will inherit what he says (ma yaquulu)﴾, meaning what is said about of wealth and children. So the meaning is: then they wish to return to enjoyment, so the freeing of (p-217) a neck.

﴿before they touch one another (min qabli an yatamassa)﴾: that is, before each of the one who made zihar and the one against whom zihar was made enjoys the other by intercourse, touching, or looking at the private part with desire. If any of that occurs before the expiation, it is obligatory upon him to seek forgiveness and not to return until he expiates. If he freed part of the neck and then touched, he must begin again, according to Abu Hanifa, may God have mercy on him.

﴿That (dhalikum)﴾: a reference to the ruling mentioned, and it is a subject whose predicate is ﴿you are admonished by it (tu'azuna bihi)﴾: that is, you are restrained by it from committing the mentioned reprehensible act, for fines are deterrents from engaging in offenses. The purpose of mentioning it is to clarify that the aim of legislating this ruling is not to compensate you with reward for your undertaking the freeing of a neck, which is a cause for great reward, but rather it is your deterrence and restraint from engaging in what necessitates it.

﴿And God is aware of what you do (bima ta'maluna)﴾: among the deeds, of which expiation and what necessitates it of the offense of zihar are part.

﴿Well-Acquainted (khabir)﴾: that is, knowing of its outward and inward aspects, and recompensing you for them. So safeguard the limits of what He has legislated for you and do not neglect any part of them.

﴿So whoever does not find﴾ — i.e., the *raqabah* (a slave, lit. "neck").

﴿then fasting for two months﴾ — i.e., then upon him is fasting for two months.

﴿consecutively, before they touch one another﴾ — at night or by day, intentionally or by mistake.

﴿So whoever is not able﴾ — i.e., to fast, for some reason among the reasons.

﴿then feeding sixty needy persons﴾ — for each needy person, half a *sa'* (a dry measure of about 2–3 kg) of wheat, or a *sa'* of something else. It is obligatory to make this payment before *al-masis* (sexual intercourse), but one does not have to start over if intercourse occurs during the feeding.

﴿That﴾ — a reference to what has preceded of the clarification, instruction of the rulings, and admonition concerning them. The sense of distance in it has been explained repeatedly. Its grammatical position is either nominative, as the subject of a *mubtada'* (inchoative), or accusative, governed by an implied verb whose cause is what follows it, i.e., "that is what occurs" or "we have done that."

﴿so that you may believe in Allah and His Messenger﴾ — and act upon His laws which He has legislated for you, and reject what you were upon in your *jahiliyyah* (pre-Islamic ignorance).

﴿And these﴾ — a reference to the rulings mentioned, and the sense of distance in it is for their magnification, as has been stated more than once.

﴿are the limits of Allah﴾ — which it is not permissible to transgress.

﴿And for the disbelievers﴾ — i.e., those who do not act upon them.

﴿is a painful punishment﴾ — He expressed it thus for emphasis, following the manner of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And whoever disbelieves, then indeed Allah is Free of need from the worlds﴾.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 58, verse 5:

﴿Indeed, those who oppose (yuhadduna) Allah and His Messenger﴾ meaning: they oppose them (yu'adduna-humā) and act in hostility toward them (yushaqqunahumā). For each of the two opposing parties, just as one is on one side and in one direction, different from the other's side and direction, so too is each in a limit (hadd) different from the other's limit. However, the use of "opposing" (al-muhadda) within the mention of the limits of Allah, rather than "enmity" (al-mu'adah) and "hostility" (al-mushaqqah), gives a beauty of placement beyond which there is no further degree.

﴿Be humiliated (kubitu)﴾ meaning: be disgraced (ukhzu). It has also been said: be forsaken (khudhilu); it has been said: be abased (udhillu); it has been said: be destroyed (uhlikū); it has been said: be cursed (lu'innu); it has been said: be enraged (ghīzu). This is what occurred on the day of the Trench (al-Khandaq). They said: the meaning of "kubitu" is: they will be humiliated, in the manner of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿The command of Allah has come﴾. It has also been said: the root of al-kabt is al-kabb (overturning).

﴿As those before them were humiliated﴾ from the disbelievers of the past nations, who were hostile to the Messengers, upon them be (p-218) prayer and peace.

﴿And We have certainly sent down clear signs﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the waw of "kubitu," meaning: they were humiliated for their opposition, while We had sent down clear, manifest signs concerning those among the nations before them who opposed Allah and His Messenger, and concerning what We did to them. It has also been said: they are signs that indicate the truthfulness and soundness of what he (ﷺ) brought.

﴿And for the disbelievers﴾ meaning: with respect to those signs, or with respect to everything that must be believed in; thus those signs enter into it first and foremost.

﴿is a humiliating punishment﴾ which takes away their honour and their arrogance.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 58, verse 6:

﴿On the Day when Allah will resurrect them all﴾ is in the accusative (manṣūb) governed either by what the preposition lām (in the phrase concerning their standing) implies, or by "humiliating" (muhīn), or by an implied verb "remember" (udhkur), to magnify the Day and to make it awesome.

﴿All together﴾ means: all of them, such that not one of them remains unresurrected, or gathered together in one single state.

﴿Then He will inform them of what they did﴾ of the abominable deeds, by making clear that they proceeded from them, or by depicting them in that (new) mode of existence in forms befitting it, awful forms, before the eyes of the witnesses, to shame them, to expose their condition, and to intensify their punishment. The words of the Exalted, ﴿Allah has counted it﴾, form a resumptive clause (isti'nāf) that comes as an answer to a question arising from what precedes it, either about the manner of the informing or about its cause, as if it were said: how will He inform them of their deeds when they are accidents (a'rāḍ) that have passed away and vanished? So it is said: Allah has counted them, a counting in which nothing escaped Him. Then the words of the Exalted, ﴿and they have forgotten it﴾, are at that point a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) relating to the object of "counted" (aḥṣā), with or without the particle qad, according to the well-known difference of opinion. Or it is said: He did not inform them of that; so it is said: Allah has counted it and they have forgotten it, and then He informs them of it, so that they may know that what they witnessed of punishment came upon them only because of it. In this there is additional reproach and censure for them beyond shame and exposure.

﴿And Allah is witness over all things﴾ nothing among affairs is ever hidden from Him. The sentence is a parenthetical concluding clause (i'tirāḍ tadhyīlī) that confirms His comprehensive counting.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 58, verse 7:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Have you not considered that Allah knows whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth?﴾ is an argument for the comprehensiveness of His knowledge, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Have you not considered the one who argued with Abraham about his Lord?﴾ and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Have you not considered that they wander in every valley?﴾ That is: Do you not know with a certain knowledge, bordering on direct observation, that He, exalted is He, knows whatever existing things are in them, whether that is by their being settled in them or by their being a part of them? His saying, exalted is He: ﴿There is no secret conversation of three but that He is their fourth...﴾ etc. is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) confirming what precedes it of the breadth of His knowledge, exalted is He, and explaining its manner. "Min" here is complete (min kana al-tammah), and it was read as "takunu" with the ta', considering that najwa (secret conversation) is feminine, though it is not a true feminine. That is: what occurs of the private conversation of three persons, that is, of their secret talk, either with najwa being annexed to thalathah, or with them being described by it, either by supposing an omitted noun, that is, "from the people of a secret conversation of three," or by making them themselves the secret conversation.

﴿Except He﴾, that is, Allah, mighty and majestic.

﴿Their fourth﴾, that is, making them four, in that He, exalted is He, joins them in being aware of it. This is an exceptive phrase (istithna' mufarragh) from the most general of circumstances.

﴿Nor five﴾: nor a secret conversation of five.

﴿Except He is their sixth﴾. The specifying of the two numbers in mention is either because of the particular occasion, for the verse was revealed concerning the secret conversation of the hypocrites, or because the speech is built upon the most common practices of those who converse secretly. The ruling was then generalized after that (p-219), so it says: ﴿Nor less than that﴾, that is, than what has been mentioned, such as one or two.

﴿Nor more﴾, such as six and what exceeds it.

﴿Except He is with them﴾, knowing what passes between them. It was also read "wa-la akthara" with the nominative, as a conjunction upon the place of "min najwa" or the place of "wa-la adna," by making "la" serve to negate the genus.

﴿Wherever they are﴾ in places, even if they are beneath the earth, for His knowledge of things is not by spatial nearness, so that it would vary with the difference of places in nearness and distance.

﴿Then He will inform them﴾. It was also read "yunbi'ahum" with the lightened form.

﴿Of what they did on the Day of Resurrection﴾, as an exposure of them and a manifestation of what necessitates their punishment.

﴿Indeed, Allah is Knowing of all things﴾, because the relation of His essence, which requires knowledge, to all things is equal.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 58, verse 8:

﴿Have you not seen those who were forbidden from secret counsel, and then return to what they were forbidden?﴾ It was revealed concerning the Jews and the hypocrites, who used to hold secret consultations among themselves and wink at one another with their eyes when they saw the believers. So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) forbade them, but they returned to the like of their deed. The address is to the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, the hamzah (interrogative particle) is for expressing wonder at their condition, and the present tense form is to indicate the repetition and renewal of their returning and to bring to mind its wondrous image. And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and they hold secret counsel in sin and transgression and disobedience to the Messenger﴾ is coordinated with what precedes it and falls under its ruling; that is, [they hold secret counsel] with what is in itself sin and is transgression against the believers, and [mutual] urging to disobey the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, by his title of Messenger. It is placed between the two addresses directed to him, peace and blessings be upon him, to increase their reproach and magnify the gravity of their disobedience. It has also been recited as "wayantajūna bil-ithmi wal-ʿudwān" with a kasra on the ʿayn, and "maʿṣiyāti al-Rasūl" (in the plural).

﴿And when they come to you, they greet you with that by which Allah has not greeted you﴾: they say "al-sāmu ʿalayka" (death be upon you), or "anʿim ṣabāḥan" (may you have a pleasant morning), while Allah, Exalted is He, says: ﴿and peace be upon the messengers﴾.

﴿And they say within themselves﴾: that is, among themselves.

﴿Why does Allah not punish us for what we say?﴾: that is, why would Allah not punish us for that, if Muhammad were a prophet?

﴿Hell is sufficient for them﴾ as punishment.

﴿They will burn therein﴾: they will enter it.

﴿And wretched is the destination﴾: that is, Hell.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 58, verse 9:

﴿O you who have believed, when you confer privately, do not confer in sin and aggression and disobedience to the Messenger﴾ in your gatherings and in your private meetings.

﴿Do not confer in sin and aggression and disobedience to the Messenger﴾ as the hypocrites do. It has been recited as "fa-la tantajū" and "fa-la tanājaw" with one of the two tā's omitted.

﴿But confer in righteousness and piety﴾ that is, in what includes the good of the believers and guarding oneself against disobedience to the Messenger, upon him be blessings and peace.

﴿And fear Allah, to whom you will be gathered﴾ alone, not to another, either independently or in association, so that He will recompense you for everything you do and everything you leave undone.

"Secret counsel is only from Satan," that is, the well-known secret conferring, which is consultation concerning sin and transgression, [it is] from Satan and not from anyone else, for he is the one who adorns it and drives people to it. And His saying, exalted is He, ﴿so that it may grieve those who believe﴾ is another statement, meaning: it is only so that it may grieve the believers, by their imagining that it is some calamity that has befallen them.

﴿But it cannot harm them at all﴾, that is, Satan or the secret conferring cannot harm the believers at all.

﴿anything﴾ of things, or any kind of harm.

﴿except by the permission of Allah﴾, that is, by His will.

﴿And upon Allah let the believers rely﴾, and let them not be concerned about their secret counsel, for He, exalted is He, will protect them from its evil.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 58, verse 11:

﴿O you who have believed, when it is said to you, "Make room (tafassahu) in the assemblies"﴾ i.e., widen (tawassa'u), and let some of you make room for others, and do not crowd one another. It derives from their saying, "Make room for me (afsih 'anni)," i.e., move aside. It was also read as "tafasahu." The phrase ﴿in the assemblies﴾ is connected to "qila" (it is said). It was read as "fi al-majlisi" (in the assembly, singular), on the basis that the intended meaning is the genus. It has also been said: the reference is to the assembly of the Messenger (ﷺ), and they used to crowd one another out, competing for nearness to him (ﷺ) and eager to hear his speech. It has also been said: it refers to an assembly of fighting, namely the positions of the warriors, as in His saying: ﴿positions for fighting﴾. It is said that a man would come to the row and say, "Make room," and they would refuse, out of their eagerness for martyrdom. It was also read as "fi al-majlasi" with a fatha on the lam, in which case it is connected definitely to "tafassahu," i.e., widen in your sitting and do not be cramped in it.

﴿So make room, and Allah will make room for you﴾ i.e., in everything you wish to have room in, of place, provision, breast, grave and other things.

﴿And when it is said, "Rise up (inshuzu)"﴾ i.e., rise up to make room for those arriving, or for what you have been commanded of prayer, jihad, or other acts of goodness.

﴿then rise up (fa-inshuzu)﴾: rise up, do not hold back, and do not neglect. It was read with a kasra on the shin.

﴿Allah will raise those of you who have believed﴾ with victory and good remembrance in this world, and with lodging in the chambers of the Gardens in the Hereafter.

﴿and those who have been given knowledge﴾ among them, in particular.

﴿by degrees﴾ high, because they have combined the two virtues of knowledge and action. Knowledge, with its elevated rank, requires action accompanied by it, which gives additional elevation that action devoid of it cannot reach, however much it may be in the utmost of righteousness. For this reason the scholar is followed in his actions, and no one else is. In the hadith: "The virtue of the scholar over the worshipper is like the virtue of the full moon on its night over the rest of the stars."

﴿And Allah is Acquainted with what you do﴾ is a warning to those who do not conform to the command. It was read "ya'malūna" with the yā' (third person).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 58, verse 12:

﴿O you who have believed, when you consult the Messenger privately, [first] present, before your private consultation, a charity.﴾ That is, [when you have a serious matter that calls for consulting him, peace and blessings be upon him].

﴿Present, before your private consultation, a charity.﴾ That is: give charity before it. (The expression "before his hands" [bayna yadayh] is a metaphor borrowed from one who has two hands.) In this command there is the honouring of the Messenger (ﷺ), benefit to the poor, a restraint against excessive questioning, and a distinction between the sincere believer and the hypocrite, and between one who loves the Hereafter and one who loves this world. It has been disputed whether this is recommended (nadb) or obligatory (wujub). However, it was abrogated by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Are you apprehensive about presenting charity before your private consultations?﴾ Although this verse is connected to it in recitation, it came down later in revelation.

It is reported from 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "There is a verse in the Book of Allah that no one acted upon except me. I had a dinar, which I exchanged, and whenever I consulted the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, I gave a dirham in charity." On the view that it is obligatory, this is understood to mean that the wealthy did not happen to hold a private consultation during the period of its validity, for it is narrated that it remained in force only for ten [days], and it has been said: only an hour.

﴿That﴾ — that is, the giving of charity.

﴿is better for you and purer﴾ — that is, for your souls, from suspicion and love of wealth. This suggests recommendation; but His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And if you do not find [the means], then indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ indicates obligation, since it is a concession for one who does not find [the means] to consult without giving charity.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 58, verse 13:**

﴿Are you apprehensive that you will offer charity before your private consultation?﴾ That is: did you fear poverty from offering charities, or did you fear offering them because of what Satan promises you of poverty, and the gathering of charities for the gathering of those addressed?

﴿So when you do not do it﴾ what you were commanded, and that was hard for you.

﴿And Allah has turned to you﴾ by permitting you not to do it. In this there is an indication that their apprehension was a sin, which Allah overlooked because He saw in them the strength of their emotional reaction, which took the place of their repentance. *Idh* here retains its original sense of the past. It has also been said that it means *idha* ("whenever"), as in His saying, ﴿when the shackles are around their necks﴾ (40:71). It has also been said that it means *in* ("if").

﴿So establish the prayer and give the zakat﴾ That is: since you neglected what you were commanded concerning offering charities, make up for it by persevering in establishing the prayer and paying the zakat.

﴿And obey Allah and His Messenger﴾ in all the other commands, for carrying them out serves as a remedy for the neglect that occurred in this matter.

﴿And Allah is All-Aware of what you do﴾ outwardly and inwardly.

﴿Have you not seen?﴾ This is an expression of wonder at the state of the hypocrites, who used to take the Jews as allies, give them counsel, and convey to them the secrets of the believers. That is, have you not looked?

﴿at those who took as allies﴾, that is, who befriended (tawallaw).

﴿a people upon whom God is angry﴾, and they are the Jews, as indicated by His saying: ﴿those whom God has cursed and with whom He is angry﴾.

﴿They are neither of you nor of them﴾, because they are hypocrites, wavering between that (between the two). The sentence is either a new sentence or a circumstantial clause (hal) from the subject of "tawallaw".

﴿And they swear falsely by God﴾, that is, they say, "By God, we are indeed Muslims." It is conjoined to "tawallaw" and falls under the wonder. The present tense (yahlifun) indicates the repetition and renewal of the oath as often as the circumstance requires. His saying, ﴿while they know﴾, is a circumstantial clause from the subject of "yahlifun", conveying the complete abomination of what they did, for swearing to what one does not know to be true is extremely vile. It indicates that lying encompasses both what the speaker knows does not correspond to reality and what he does not know.

It was narrated that he, peace and blessings be upon him, was in one of his chambers and said: "A man is about to enter upon you now, whose heart is the heart of a tyrant and who looks with the eye of a devil." Then Abdullah ibn Nabtal, the hypocrite, entered, and he was blue-eyed. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to him: "Why do you and your companions revile me?" He swore by God that he had not done so. Then the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "You did." (p-222) He left and brought his companions, and they swore by God that they had not reviled him. Then the verse was revealed.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 58, verse 15:

﴿Allah has prepared for them﴾ because of that.

﴿a severe punishment﴾ a kind of punishment that is intensifying.

﴿Indeed, evil is what they have been doing﴾ in the past, over a long span of time, so they became accustomed to evil conduct, were harmed by it, and persisted in it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 58, verse 16:

﴿They have taken their oaths as a shield﴾: the false oaths which they swear when there is need, and it is read with a kasra on the hamza (إيمانَهُمْ, "their faith" or "their oath" in the sense of their professed faith), meaning: their faith which they displayed to the people of Islam.

﴿A shield﴾ (جُنَّةً): a protection and a cover behind which they guard their blood and their property. The "taking" (ittikhadh) according to this reading is an expression for concealing themselves with what they displayed in deed. As for according to the first reading, it is an expression for their preparing their false oaths and readying them until the time of need, so that they may swear by them and be freed from being held to account, not an expression for using them in deed; for that comes after being held to account, which is preceded by the occurrence of the crime and the betrayal, and the taking of a shield must precede being held to account and be its cause as well, as the fa' (ف) in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿so they barred﴾ (فَصَدُّوا), indicates, meaning: the people.

﴿From the way of Allah﴾ (عَنْ سَبِيلِ اللَّهِ): during their security, by discouraging those they meet from entering Islam and by weakening the matter of the Muslims in their eyes.

﴿For them is a humiliating punishment﴾ (فَلَهم عَذابٌ مُهِينٌ): a second threat, with another description of their punishment. It has been said: the first is the punishment of the grave, or the punishment of the Hereafter.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 58, verse 17:

﴿Their wealth and their children will not avail them at all against God.﴾ That is, against His punishment, exalted is He.

﴿Anything﴾ of what could be called availing. It is related that a man among them said: "We will certainly be helped on the Day of Resurrection by our selves, our wealth and our children."

﴿Those﴾ are the ones described by the ugly qualities that have been mentioned.

﴿Are the companions of the Fire﴾: that is, those who are constantly bound to it and accompany it.

﴿They will abide therein forever﴾: they will never come out of it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 58, verse 18:

﴿The day Allah raises them all up together﴾ It has been said: this is an adverbial clause (zarf) modifying His saying, Exalted is He: "For them there is a humiliating punishment."

﴿Then they will swear to Him﴾ That is, to Allah, Exalted is He, on that Day, that they are Muslims.

﴿as they swear to you﴾ In this world.

﴿And they think﴾ in the Hereafter.

﴿that they are﴾ by those profane oaths.

﴿upon something﴾ of bringing about some benefit or warding off some harm, as they were in this world, when they used to ward off with them (the oaths) their lives and their property, and used to draw by them worldly advantages.

﴿Verily, it is they who are the liars﴾ those who exaggerate in lying to a point beyond which there is no further aspiration, in that they dared to lie in the presence of the Knower of the unseen, and supposed that their profane oaths would pass off falsehood before Him just as they pass it off before the heedless.

(p-223) ﴿Al-Shaytan has taken possession of them﴾, i.e., he gained control over them, from "ḥudtu al-ibil" (I gathered the camels), when you gain control over them and herd them together. It is among the verbs that came according to their original form, like "istaṣwaba" and "istanwaqa," i.e., he possessed them.

﴿So He caused them to forget the remembrance of Allah﴾, to the extent that they did not remember Him in their hearts nor with their tongues.

﴿Those﴾, who are described with the abominations mentioned, are the party of Shaytan, his troops, and his followers.

﴿Surely the party of Shaytan, they are the losers﴾, i.e., those described with a loss beyond which there is no end, in that they forfeited for themselves the everlasting bliss and took in its place the painful punishment. In opening the sentence with the two particles of alertness and affirmation, and in placing the two annexed nouns explicitly in a position where a pronoun would be expected, according to one of the two views, and in inserting the separating pronoun, there are forms of emphasis that are not hidden.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 58, verse 20:

﴿Indeed, those who oppose Allah and His Messenger﴾ is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) brought to give the reason for what precedes it, namely the loss of the party of Satan. He expressed them by the relative pronoun (al-mawsul) to draw attention to what is contained in the relative clause (sila), indicating that showing affection to one who opposes Allah and His Messenger is itself opposition to them both, and to signal the cause (ʿilla) of the ruling.

﴿Those﴾ — for what they did of turning away and showing affection (to the opposers).

﴿Among the most humiliated﴾ — that is, among the company of those who are the most abased of Allah's creation, of the earlier and the later ones, because the abasement of one of two opponents is in proportion to the might of the other. Since the might of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is without limit, the abasement of those who oppose Him is likewise.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 58, verse 21:

﴿Allah has decreed﴾ is a resumptive clause (istి'naf, a new sentence) that serves to give the reason for their being among the most abased. That is: He has decreed and established it in the Preserved Tablet (al-lawh, the Preserved Tablet). Since this takes the place of an oath (qasam), it is answered with what is used to answer an oath, so it says: ﴿Assuredly I shall prevail, I and My messengers﴾, that is, by argument and by the sword and what is similar to them, or by one of the two. A parallel to this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And certainly Our word has already preceded for Our servants, the messengers. Indeed, they would be the ones given victory. And indeed, Our soldiers – they will be the victorious﴾. It has also been read "wa-rusulī" with the ya' vowelled with a fatha (i.e., "wa-rusulíya" as a variant reading in which the final ya' is pronounced with fatha).

﴿Indeed, Allah is Powerful﴾ over granting victory to His prophets.

﴿Almighty﴾, not overcome in His purpose.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 58, verse 22:**

﴿You will not find a people who believe in God and the Last Day﴾. The address is either to the Prophet (ﷺ) or to every individual. The verb "تَجِدُ" (tajidu, "you find") may be transitive to two objects, in which case His saying, ﴿who show affection to those who oppose God and His Messenger﴾, is its second object. Or it may be transitive to one object, in which case it is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) referring to its object, because that object is specified by the attribute. It has also been said that it is another attribute of "قَوْمًا" (qawman, "a people"), meaning: a people who combine belief in God and the Last Day with showing affection to the enemies of God and His Messenger. The purpose of negating "الوِجْدان" (al-wijdān, "finding") is to negate the affection itself, in the sense that it should not come to be, and its proper state is that it be prevented and never found in any circumstance, even if everyone strives earnestly to seek it.

﴿Even if they were﴾, i.e., those who oppose God and His Messenger. The plural is used in view of the meaning of "مَن" (man, "whoever"), just as the singular is used earlier in view of its wording.

﴿their fathers﴾: the fathers of those who show affection.

﴿or their sons, or their brothers, or their kindred﴾. The requirement of belief in God, exalted is He, is that one forsake all of them entirely. The discussion of "لَوْ" (law, "even if") has been detailed several times before.

﴿Those﴾ is a reference to those whom they do not show affection to, even if they are the closest of people to them and most closely related by kinship. The sense of distance in the demonstrative is for the elevation of their rank in virtue. It is a subject (mubtadaʾ) whose predicate is ﴿He has written faith in their hearts﴾, i.e., He has established it in them. It is written there definitively, and no deed of the limbs is established in the heart.

﴿and has strengthened them﴾, i.e., He has fortified them.

﴿with a spirit from Him﴾, i.e., from God, exalted is He. It is the light of the heart, or the Qur'an, or victory over the enemy. It was also said that the pronoun refers to faith, because hearts are given life by it, so "مِن" (min) is partitive/abstractive (tajrīdiyya). His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and He will admit them﴾ etc., is an explanation of the effects of His mercy in the Hereafter after the explanation of His worldly kindnesses, i.e., and He will admit them into the Hereafter.

﴿gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever﴾, forever and ever. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿God is pleased with them﴾ is a resumptive clause functioning as a justification for what He has bestowed upon them of the effects of His mercy, both immediate and deferred. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and they are pleased with Him﴾ explains their delight in what they have been given, both immediately and in the future. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Those are the party of God﴾ is an honouring of them by explaining that they are specially His. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Surely the party of God are the successful﴾ explains their being specially granted success in the bliss of both abodes, and the discussion of embellishing the sentence with various forms of emphasis is as has passed in similar cases.

From the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever recites Surah al-Mujadila, he will be written among the party of God on the Day of Resurrection."
